subject: religious-studies
topicDisplay: Religious Ethical Teachings About Medical Ethics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which statement reflects a religious argument used against euthanasia?
options: Doctors must never help patients
Only God should decide the time of death, as life is sacred
Suffering should always be maximised
Life has no value
questions.explain: Some believers argue that, since life is God-given, only God should decide when it ends.

questions.q: Which position is described as 'pro-choice' in the abortion debate?
options: The view that all life begins at birth only
The view that doctors should decide for everyone
The view that abortion should never be allowed
The view that a woman should have the right to choose whether to continue a pregnancy
questions.explain: The pro-choice position emphasises a woman's right to decide about her own pregnancy.

questions.q: Which scientific theory describes how living things change over many generations through natural selection?
options: The cosmological argument
The design argument
The theory of evolution
The sanctity of life
questions.explain: Evolution by natural selection, associated with Charles Darwin, explains how species change over time.

questions.q: What does the Genesis creation account say God did on the seventh day?
options: Rested
Separated light from darkness
Created the stars
Created human beings
questions.explain: In Genesis, God rests on the seventh day, which is linked to the idea of the Sabbath as a day of rest.

questions.q: Which view supports the use of animals in some circumstances within many religious traditions?
options: That animals are worthless
That animals have no role in creation
That humans have stewardship over animals and may use them responsibly
That animals must never be touched
questions.explain: Many traditions allow responsible use of animals while still teaching kindness and care towards them.

questions.q: Which religion is particularly associated with the principle of 'ahimsa' (non-harm to living things)?
options: Hinduism (and Jainism and Buddhism)
Only Islam
Only Christianity
No religion teaches this
questions.explain: Ahimsa, the principle of non-violence towards all living beings, is central to Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism.

questions.q: What does the term 'sanctity of life' mean?
options: That only human achievement matters
That life is purely a matter of chance
That life is sacred and God-given, and should be respected
That life has no special value
questions.explain: Sanctity of life is the belief that life is holy, God-given and deserving of special respect.

questions.q: Which is a non-religious (e.g. Humanist) view on the origins of the universe?
options: The universe does not exist
God personally shaped each planet
The universe arose through natural processes such as the Big Bang, without a creator
The universe was created in six literal days
questions.explain: Humanists generally explain the universe through scientific processes rather than a divine creator.

questions.q: What does the Christian idea of 'dominion' over creation traditionally mean?
options: Humans may destroy nature freely
Nature has authority over humans
Humans are given responsibility and authority to care for creation
Humans must never use natural resources
questions.explain: Dominion is often interpreted as responsible authority and care, not the right to exploit.

questions.q: What is the difference between active and passive euthanasia?
options: Active is always legal and passive is always illegal
Passive euthanasia is a form of fertility treatment
Active involves doing something to end life; passive involves withdrawing or withholding treatment
They mean exactly the same thing
questions.explain: Active euthanasia means taking direct action to end life, while passive euthanasia means allowing death by stopping treatment.

questions.q: What is a common misconception about evolution and religion?
options: That the debate is genuinely complex
That Christians hold differing views on this
That accepting evolution always means rejecting God
That some believers accept both evolution and God
questions.explain: Many religious believers accept evolution as the process through which God created life, so the two need not conflict.

questions.q: Why might a religious believer object to using animals in cosmetic testing?
options: Because cosmetics are forbidden
Because animals have no place in creation
Because causing unnecessary suffering conflicts with the duty to treat creation with care
Because animals cannot feel anything
questions.explain: Many believers oppose testing that causes needless animal suffering, as stewardship calls for kindness to creation.

questions.q: Which of these is a reason a believer might give for opposing pollution and waste?
options: The Earth belongs only to humans to exploit
Pollution improves creation
Damaging the planet fails in the God-given duty of stewardship
Future generations do not matter
questions.explain: Believers often argue that polluting the Earth neglects the responsibility to care for God's creation.

questions.q: What is 'euthanasia'?
options: The painless ending of a life to relieve suffering
A type of fertility treatment
A medical examination
A funeral ceremony
questions.explain: Euthanasia refers to deliberately ending a life, usually to relieve incurable suffering.

questions.q: Which religious concept teaches that humans should care for the environment as carers, not owners?
options: Materialism
Dominion as exploitation
Stewardship
Indifference
questions.explain: Stewardship is the belief that humans have a duty to look after the Earth on God's behalf.

questions.q: How might a religious believer reconcile belief in creation with the Big Bang theory?
options: By denying the universe exists
By claiming science and faith can never overlap in any way
By rejecting all science
By suggesting God could be the cause behind the Big Bang
questions.explain: Many believers argue the Big Bang could be the means by which God created the universe, so the two can coexist.

questions.q: Which biblical idea is often used to support human responsibility for the environment?
options: Humans were placed in the garden 'to work it and take care of it'
Nature exists only to be destroyed
Humans should ignore the natural world
Animals must be worshipped
questions.explain: Genesis describes humans being given the garden to tend and care for, supporting the idea of stewardship.

questions.q: What is 'abortion'?
options: The deliberate ending of a pregnancy before birth
A ceremony to name a child
A treatment to help couples conceive
The natural birth of a baby
questions.explain: Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy, a deeply debated ethical issue.

questions.q: Why might some religious believers oppose certain fertility treatments?
options: Because they replace the need for families
Because they always fail
Because they may involve discarding unused embryos, raising sanctity-of-life concerns
Because they are illegal
questions.explain: Some object where embryos are destroyed, viewing this as conflicting with the sanctity of life.

questions.q: Which view best describes the religious idea of 'quality of life'?
options: Life only matters if a person is wealthy
The idea that the level of wellbeing and dignity in a life can be considered
Life has no value of any kind
A life's value depends only on its length
questions.explain: Quality of life considers the wellbeing, comfort and dignity of a life, sometimes weighed against sanctity of life.

questions.q: Which view best reflects a 'pro-life' position on abortion?
options: That the foetus is not alive at any stage
That the unborn child has a right to life from conception
That abortion is always the woman's free choice
That life only begins at adulthood
questions.explain: The pro-life position holds that human life begins at conception and should be protected.

questions.q: What is 'IVF' an example of?
options: A form of capital punishment
A type of euthanasia
A fertility treatment helping couples conceive
An environmental policy
questions.explain: IVF (in-vitro fertilisation) is a fertility treatment that helps couples who struggle to conceive.
